chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Umar ibn Udhaynah, from Ismail ibn al-Fadl al-Hashimi, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about Mut'ah (temporary marriage), so he said: 'Meet Abdul Malik ibn Jurayj and ask him about it, for he has knowledge of it from us.' So I met him and he dictated to me much regarding its permissibility. Among what Ibn Jurayj narrated to me was that he said: 'There is no time limit nor a number [limit] in it. Rather, she is at the status of slave girls. He may marry from them as many as he wishes, and the one with four wives may marry from them as many as he wishes, without a guardian and without witnesses. So when the term expires, she becomes divorced from him without a formal divorce pronouncement, and he gives her a small amount, and her waiting period is two menstruations. And if she does not menstruate, then it is forty-five days.'
So I came to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) with the book and presented it to him, and he said: 'He is truthful and I confirm it.'

Ibn Udhaynah said: 'And Zurarah ibn A'yan used to say this and swore that it is the truth, except that he used to say: If she menstruates, then it is one menstruation, and if she does not menstruate, then it is a month and a half.'
ai.seo_question: What are the rules regarding duration, number of wives, and waiting period in Shia temporary marriage (Mut'ah)?
ai.summary: This narration from Al-Kafi establishes the permissibility of Mut'ah by citing Imam al-Sadiq’s verification of Ibn Jurayj’s report, which equates the contractual simplicity of temporary marriage to that of slave girls—requiring no guardian or witnesses and allowing unlimited simultaneous partners. The text highlights a scholarly nuance regarding the 'iddah (waiting period), contrasting the primary ruling of two menstruations with Zarrar ibn A'yn’s affirmed opinion of one menstruation or forty-five days, underscoring the flexibility in jurisprudential derivation within the Shia tradition.
